Unlike gasoline and diesel, Jet A consumption continues to increase, illustrating the need for solutions to increase domestic fuel production and reduce aircraft emissions (EIA 2025d). Therefore, research and development of alternative energy carriers is necessary to enable flexibility for the aviation industry to meet demand with domestically produced fuels. Figure 1 shows U.S. crude oil production and inputs to refineries. The difference between domestic crude production and crude input to refineries is supplied by imports (EIA 2025f, 2025g). The jet fuel share of refinery output increased in the past two years compared with previous years, indicating that refineries are adjusting jet fuel output—likely a result of increased demand for jet fuel as gasoline and diesel decline (EIA 2025h). Figure 2 shows a balanced market where domestic jet fuel production exceeds consumption in 8 out of the past 10 years (EIA 2025d, 2025h). Increased domestic production of alternative energy carriers for aviation could reduce reliance on crude oil imports. The United States both imports and exports Jet A, driven by the location of refineries and availability and capacity of infrastructure to move fuels to airports.
